Domaine de la Romanée-Conti
places.blurb: The Vosne-Romanée domaine that owns Romanée-Conti and La Tâche outright and holds pieces of Richebourg, Échezeaux, Grands Échezeaux, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and Montrachet.

places.name: Domaine Leroy
places.blurb: Twenty-three hectares of mostly premier and grand cru Burgundy, farmed biodynamically since Lalou Bize-Leroy assembled the domaine in 1988 out of Charles Noëllat's holdings.

places.name: Maison Joseph Drouhin
places.blurb: Beaune house founded in 1880, certified organic across its own vineyards from the 2009 vintage, and the family that took Burgundy's argument to Oregon in 1987.

places.name: Maison Louis Jadot
places.blurb: A Beaune négociant founded in 1859, farming and buying across 270 hectares of Burgundy including Beaujolais crus, and bottling nothing that is not an appellation wine.

places.name: Chambertin
places.blurb: Gevrey's grand cru on the mid-slope, and the name the village bolted onto its own in 1847 — the first commune in Burgundy to do it, and the start of every double-barrelled name on the Côte.

places.name: Clos de Vougeot
places.blurb: Fifty hectares behind a wall the Cistercians of Cîteaux built, and more than eighty owners inside it. One name on every label, and a slope that runs from grand cru ground at the top to heavy clay by the road.

places.name: Corton
places.blurb: The hill above Aloxe, and Burgundy's largest grand cru: 95 hectares in production, nearly all of it red, and the only red grand cru on the Côte de Beaune.

places.name: La Tâche
places.blurb: Five hectares in Vosne-Romanée, one owner, about 12,700 bottles. The appellation rules set 35 hl/ha, 9,000 vines to the hectare and 11.5% potential alcohol before anyone picks.

places.name: Musigny
places.blurb: Ten hectares above Chambolle, the one grand cru of the Côte de Nuits that also makes a white — about two thirds of a hectare of it.

places.name: Richebourg
places.blurb: Vosne-Romanée grand cru north of Romanée-Conti, on deeper soil, giving the broadest wine of that group of neighbours.

places.name: Romanée-Conti
places.blurb: Under two hectares of Vosne-Romanée hillside, held by one owner, producing about 3,500 bottles a year. No other patch of ground in wine carries this much argument per square metre.

Felton Road
places.blurb: Bannockburn, Central Otago — schist, old gold workings, and a cellar that farms organically and biodynamically and bottles its blocks separately.

places.name: Rippon
places.blurb: Vines on a lake terrace at Wanaka, biodynamic, with the Southern Alps behind them — the photograph that sells Central Otago, and a family that has farmed the slope since the nineteenth century.

places.name: Ackerman Family Vineyards at the Ackerman Heritage House
Ackerman Family Vineyards at the Ackerman Heritage House
Carr Winery - The Santa Ynez Warehouse
de Vine Wine & Beer and Food
Eric K. James Vineyards Tasting Room
Eric K. James Vineyards Tasting Room
Los Olivos Tasting Room & Wine Shop
A Tribute to Grace Wine Company
Au Bon Climat
places.blurb: Founded in 1982 by Jim Clendenen and Adam Tolmach, and housed inside Bien Nacido since. Clendenen ran it alone from 1990 and made Santa Barbara pinot noir something people ordered by name.

places.name: Beauregard Vineyards Tasting Room and Winery
Bien Nacido & Solomon Hills Estates Tasting Room
Calera
places.blurb: Josh Jensen went looking for limestone in California because Burgundy grows on it, found a lime kiln site high on Mount Harlan in San Benito County, and planted pinot noir at 2,200 feet in 1975.

places.name: Hanzell Vineyards
places.blurb: James Zellerbach planted two acres of pinot noir and four of chardonnay above Sonoma in 1953, then built a cellar copying Burgundy's methods — French oak, temperature control, inert gas.

places.name: Refugio Ranch Vineyards - Los Olivos Tasting Room
Williams Selyem
places.blurb: Burt Williams and Ed Selyem started in a Forestville garage in the early 1980s, bought fruit from Russian River growers and put the vineyard's name on the label.

places.name: Adelsheim Vineyard
places.blurb: David and Ginny Adelsheim bought 19 acres outside Newberg in 1971. He then spent decades on the committee work — the AVA petitions, the clone imports, the arguments about what Oregon should be allowed to call itself.

places.name: Domaine Drouhin Oregon
places.blurb: Burgundy's answer to the 1979 tasting: the Drouhin family bought land in the Dundee Hills in 1987 and built a gravity-flow winery into the slope, with Véronique Drouhin making the wine.

places.name: Lachini Vineyards - Tasting Barn and Estate Vineyard
Methven Family Vineyards Dundee Tasting Room
Purple Hands Winery and Urban Tasting Room
Sokol Blosser
places.blurb: Bill Blosser and Susan Sokol Blosser planted five acres of pinot noir into a former prune orchard in 1971 and made their first vintage in 1977. The estate has been certified organic since 2005.

places.name: The Eyrie Vineyards
places.blurb: David and Diana Lett planted the Willamette Valley's first pinot noir in 1965 and made their first vintage in 1970. They also made the first American pinot gris.

places.name: Winter's Hill Estate Vinearyd and Winery
Bien Nacido
places.blurb: Eight hundred acres on the Santa Maria bench, planted in 1969 and farmed row by row for whoever buys the rows. Over 250 acres of it is pinot noir, and the vineyard's name appears on more labels than most wineries manage.

places.name: Sanford & Benedict
places.blurb: The planting that proved the Santa Ynez river gap: put in during 1971 by Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict on a north-facing slope nobody else wanted, and now inside the Sta. Rita Hills AVA.
